title: Isolated Bilateral Ptosis as an Early Sign of Guillain-Barré Syndrome
case_prompt:
A 30-year-old woman presented with a one-week history of progressive, painless drooping of both eyelids. The ptosis began in the left eye and five days later involved the right eye. She also reported generalized malaise, fatigability with routine activities, and mild difficulties with hand dexterity and walking. There was no history of flu-like illness or gastrointestinal infection, and no diurnal variation in symptoms. Her medical history was unremarkable.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Mental status was intact. There was bilateral ptosis with inability to open the eyelids voluntarily; on upward gaze, there was mild lid elevation. Pupils were equal and reactive to light, extraocular movements were full in all directions, and Bell’s phenomenon was preserved. The remainder of the cranial nerve and sensory examinations was normal. Muscle strength, tone, coordination, and gait were normal, but deep tendon reflexes were absent in all limbs.

Initial laboratory studies, including a complete blood count and metabolic panel (renal, liver, and thyroid function tests; electrolytes; and glucose), were normal. Testing for ocular myasthenia gravis included an edrophonium challenge, which was negative, and repetitive supramaximal nerve stimulation on day 9, which did not reveal a decremental response. Cerebrospinal fluid obtained on day 9 showed a protein concentration of 0.6 g/L (reference range, 0.15–0.45 g/L) with fewer than 5 white cells per microliter and a normal glucose level; CSF cultures and viral studies were negative. Serum assays for anti-GQ1b, antiganglioside, and anti–acetylcholine receptor antibodies performed on day 12 were negative. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Myasthenia gravis was excluded because edrophonium testing was negative and repetitive stimulation failed to show a decremental response — “Since ocular myasthenia gravis needed to be ruled out, an edrophonium test was performed but was negative, and repetitive supramaximal stimulation ... did not show a decremental response.”  
2. Botulism was ruled out by preserved autonomic pupillary function — “The preservation of autonomic pupillary function excludes botulism intoxication.”  
3. Central and oculomotor pathway lesions were excluded on the basis of normal neuroimaging — “Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain was normal.”  
4. Miller Fisher syndrome was considered but made unlikely by early albuminocytologic dissociation, absence of anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies, and lack of ophthalmoplegia — “there were several findings which supported the diagnosis of a variant of GBS over Miller Fisher syndrome: firstly, the presence of albuminocytological dissociation in the first week, which is unusual for Miller Fisher syndrome; secondly, the absence of anti-GQ1b IgG antibodies; and finally, the clinical course, namely, the absence of opthalmoplegia throughout the course.”  
5. Acute ophthalmoparesis without ataxia (AO) was excluded due to absence of external ophthalmoplegia and negative anti-GQ1b antibodies — “In AO, one of the so-called anti-GQ1b IgG antibody syndromes, the most common manifestation is external ophthalmoplegia (bilateral abduction deficit), followed by oculomotor nerve involvement, internal ophthalmoplegia, and finally ptosis which is not the case here.”  
6. Bickerstaff brain stem encephalitis was excluded because the patient did not meet its diagnostic criteria — “the patient did not fulfil the criteria for Miller Fisher syndrome, GBS with ophthalmoplegia, Bickerstaff's brain stem encephalitis or acute ophthalmoparesis without ataxia (AO).”
